question: Can each supervised concept be represented by an input-dependent vector rather than one scalar, preserving concept interventions while escaping the usual task-accuracy cost of a concept bottleneck?

key_findings.claim: CEM replaces each scalar bottleneck concept with a learned positive/negative embedding pair, mixes the pair with a supervised concept probability, and concatenates the mixed embeddings for task prediction.
key_findings.evidence: For concept i, two input-dependent m-dimensional generators produce positive and negative embeddings; a shared scoring function predicts p_i, and the downstream representation is p_i c_i+ + (1-p_i)c_i-. At intervention time p_i is set to the binary concept label, while RandInt exposes the model to random oracle interventions during training with probability 0.25.

anchors.section: 3.1 Architecture and 3.2 Intervening with Concept Embeddings

key_findings.claim: The reported predictive gains are real on the paper's benchmarks but are largest precisely where the vector bottleneck can carry label-relevant information not captured by the named concepts.
key_findings.evidence: On CUB, CEM reaches 77.11% task accuracy versus 73.41% for a no-concept model, 72.98% for Fuzzy-CBM, and 70.70% for Hybrid-CBM. On the deliberately concept-incomplete 256-class CelebA task it reaches 30.63% versus 26.80%, 25.07%, and 30.24%; on Dot it reaches 97.13% while scalar Boolean and Fuzzy CBMs stay near 48%. A linear probe predicts held-out CUB concepts from CEM embeddings at 94.33% versus 91.83% from Hybrid-CBM embeddings.

anchors.section: Appendix A.9 Bottleneck Representation Experiment Details

key_findings.claim: The assertion that concept supervision covers the whole embedding is not technically established: only a scalar score of each input-dependent vector is directly supervised, leaving many task-optimized degrees of freedom that need not be concept-exclusive.
key_findings.evidence: The concept loss is applied to p_i, a shared scorer's scalar output, whereas the m-dimensional positive and negative generators also receive downstream task gradients. Two inputs with the same concept labels can therefore retain different task-relevant embeddings. The paper's class-coherent nearest neighbors and successful held-out-concept probes demonstrate this extra information; they support usefulness but contradict a strict human-readable bottleneck interpretation.

key_findings.claim: Concept Alignment Score is an informative clustering diagnostic but is not a sufficient measure of concept faithfulness or causal reliance.
key_findings.evidence: CAS averages ground-truth concept-label homogeneity after k-medoids clustering over many cluster counts. The no-concept black box scores 82.12 on CUB, above Boolean-CBM's 81.18 and Fuzzy-CBM's 80.79, which the authors attribute to class-concept correlations. The metric can reward correlated class structure, capacity, and increasingly fine clusters without testing whether one concept's representation is exclusive, stable, or causally used.

key_findings.claim: The information-plane experiment does not isolate an escape from an information bottleneck because representation dimension and injected-noise convention change across models.
key_findings.evidence: The analysis uses a Gaussian-kernel upper bound after adding noise to deterministic continuous activations. Scalar CBMs have dimension k while CEM has dimension km, and the authors set noise variance to representation dimension divided by 100. Consequently the plotted mutual-information values depend on both capacity and an ad hoc dimension-dependent noise scale, so they are not a like-for-like proof that CEM uniquely overcomes a bottleneck.

Appendix A.2, The role of noise

key_findings.claim: CEM responds strongly to oracle corrections and remains more robust than scalar CBMs to deliberately wrong interventions, but the evaluation does not establish benefit under realistic human errors or distribution shift.
key_findings.evidence: Randomly correcting more ground-truth concepts increases CUB and CelebA accuracy, while wrong corrections degrade all models and CEM degrades more slowly. The intervention values and concept choices are oracle-generated; there is no human study, annotation-cost model, selective-query policy, correlated-error model, or out-of-distribution evaluation. Residual task information in the vectors can itself make wrong interventions less damaging.

method.core_idea: Give each named concept an input-dependent positive and negative vector state, then use a supervised scalar probability to interpolate between those states before task prediction.
method.mechanism: A backbone produces a latent code; per-concept generators map it to two m-dimensional vectors; a shared scorer converts each pair into a concept probability; the probability-weighted vectors are concatenated and passed to a linear task head. Joint task and concept losses train the whole network, and test-time interventions replace the probability with an oracle binary concept value.
assumptions: Named binary concepts and their labels are available for at least part of training.
A scalar scorer is enough to align the relevant parts of both concept embeddings with the intended semantics.
Task-relevant residual information inside a concept vector is compatible with the desired notion of interpretability.
Random oracle corrections during training approximate the interventions expected at deployment.
Clustering homogeneity and information-plane estimates are suitable proxies for concept alignment and retained information.

techniques.role: Represent the active and inactive states of every binary concept with separate input-dependent vectors.
Interpolate the two vectors using a supervised scalar concept probability.
Clamp the mixture weight to a known binary concept value at test time.
Regularize the model by randomly applying ground-truth interventions during training.
Estimate concept alignment from k-medoids cluster homogeneity over a range of cluster counts.
Compare noisy KDE upper bounds on representation mutual information with inputs, labels, and concepts.

evaluations.setting: XOR, Trigonometry, Dot, CUB-200, and a constructed concept-incomplete CelebA task; five seeds and Box-Cox 95% confidence intervals.
evaluations.result: CEM reports 77.11% on CUB, 30.63% on CelebA, and 97.13% on Dot.
evaluations.baseline: No-concept models report 73.41%, 26.80%, and 97.57%; Hybrid-CBM reports 70.70%, 30.24%, and 96.67%.

evaluations.setting: The same five tasks with representations clustered across multiple k-medoids resolutions.
evaluations.result: CEM reports 86.14 on CUB, 79.47 on CelebA, and 95.98 on Dot.
evaluations.baseline: Hybrid-CBM reports 83.19, 77.48, and 72.66; the no-concept model reports 82.12, 71.66, and 57.31.

evaluations.setting: CUB with only 25% of concept annotations used to train CEM and Hybrid-CBM; linear probes predict the remaining 75% concepts.
evaluations.result: CEM bottlenecks yield 94.33% plus or minus 0.88 while maintaining roughly 77% task accuracy.
evaluations.baseline: Hybrid-CBM bottlenecks yield 91.83% plus or minus 0.51 with comparable task accuracy.

evaluations.setting: CUB and CelebA with increasing numbers of randomly selected correct or incorrect oracle interventions.
evaluations.result: CEM improves with correct interventions and is more tolerant of a small number of incorrect interventions than scalar CBMs.
evaluations.baseline: Hybrid-CBM changes little under correct interventions; Boolean and Fuzzy CBMs collapse more quickly under wrong ones.

limitations: Author-stated: the extra embedding generators increase computation, though measured large-dataset epoch time is reported as under 10% above vanilla CBMs.
Author-stated: simple Euclidean neighbor visualizations may not capture the learned geometry, and information should ideally be assigned to interpretable semantic factors.
Reviewer inference: an input-dependent vector per concept is a soft information channel, not a strict bottleneck whose complete contents are human-readable or fully supervised.
Reviewer inference: CelebA is intentionally constructed so omitted attributes remain necessary for a 256-class target, directly favoring information leakage through the embeddings.
Reviewer inference: CAS and the mutual-information experiment are capacity- and correlation-sensitive and do not establish concept exclusivity or causal faithfulness.
Reviewer inference: interventions are oracle, random, in-distribution, and cost-free; realistic human selection, uncertainty, mistakes, and distribution shift are absent.
Reviewer inference: only five seeds are used, and the headline benchmark suite contains two synthetic tasks and two image datasets rather than broad domains or high-stakes settings.
failure_modes: The task head can exploit class, nuisance, or missing-concept information stored in concept vectors even when scalar concept predictions are correct.
An intervention can switch the mixture weight while preserving sample-specific residual information in the selected embedding, so it may not mean what a user expects concept replacement to mean.
Under distribution shift, leakage learned from training correlations can poison interventions and make corrections move predictions in the wrong direction.
Concept clustering can look coherent because of class correlation rather than because each vector isolates the named concept.
Larger embedding dimension can improve accuracy while progressively weakening auditability and increasing the number of unidentifiable representations.
reusable_insights: A richer interface can retain a supervised scalar control while giving the predictor additional capacity, but capacity and interpretability must then be measured separately.
Successful intervention responsiveness is not the same as semantic faithfulness; tests should check invariance within a concept state and exclusivity across concepts.
Probe recoverability is double-edged evidence: it demonstrates useful structure while also revealing information channels beyond the declared bottleneck.
Evaluation of concept interfaces should include realistic intervention policies, human error, annotation cost, and distribution shift rather than only oracle corrections.
Representation comparisons based on mutual information need dimension-matched estimators and prespecified noise conventions.
open_questions: Can concept embeddings be made canonical or factorized so that within-concept variation is bounded and explicitly interpretable?
How much task accuracy remains after adversarially removing label and other-concept information conditional on the declared concept?
Do people make better, faster, or safer corrections with CEMs than with scalar CBMs when concept labels are uncertain and costly?
Which intervention-aware training objective remains reliable under correlated mistakes and out-of-distribution leakage?
Can alignment metrics jointly test semantic purity, causal use, intervention locality, and representation stability?

competitive_landscape.title: Do Concept Bottleneck Models Learn as Intended?
competitive_landscape.difference: This study shows that concept-supervised bottlenecks can fail to ground concepts in their intended inputs; CEM adds vector capacity but does not directly eliminate that semantic-identification problem.

competitive_landscape.title: Addressing Leakage in Concept Bottleneck Models
competitive_landscape.difference: This NeurIPS 2022 work treats unintended information leakage as a failure to control in CBMs, whereas CEM intentionally uses additional within-concept capacity to recover accuracy and interprets the structure post hoc.

competitive_landscape.title: Learning to Receive Help: Intervention-Aware Concept Embedding Models
competitive_landscape.difference: IntCEM jointly learns an intervention policy and trains for sequential help, addressing the original paper's random oracle selection protocol but retaining its dynamic concept embeddings.

competitive_landscape.title: Eliminating Information Leakage in Hard Concept Bottleneck Models with Supervised, Hierarchical Concept Learning
competitive_landscape.difference: SupCBM treats leakage as something to remove through supervised hierarchical concept learning, offering the opposite design trade-off to CEM's deliberately expressive per-concept vectors.

competitive_landscape.title: On the Concept Trustworthiness in Concept Bottleneck Models
competitive_landscape.difference: ProtoCBM adds spatially grounded prototypical concepts and explicitly evaluates whether learned evidence supports each concept, targeting a dimension of trustworthiness that CEM's cluster-homogeneity score does not test.

competitive_landscape.title: Avoiding Leakage Poisoning: Concept Interventions Under Distribution Shifts
competitive_landscape.difference: MixCEM directly studies leakage poisoning under shift and modifies concept embeddings to make interventions safer, exposing a deployment failure mode not evaluated in the original CEM paper.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: CEM is presented as a concept bottleneck architecture that overcomes the accuracy-interpretability trade-off by replacing scalar concepts with semantically aligned embeddings while preserving interventions.
novelty_assessment.evidence: The dual-embedding mixture, CAS metric, five-task evaluation, oracle intervention experiments, representation probes, and embedding-size ablations substantiate the architectural contribution and benchmark gains.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: The architectural novelty is clear and influential, and the experiments show a practical accuracy-intervention trade-off. The stronger claim of preserving bottleneck interpretability is not established: the method recovers performance by opening an input-dependent vector channel whose task-relevant contents are neither fully concept-supervised nor human-readable. Later work on leakage, intervention policies, spatial grounding, and distribution shift makes that distinction central rather than incidental.

reviewer_notes: Read all 26 extracted pages, including the complete appendix. Rendered and inspected the architecture, information-plane plots, nearest-neighbor panels, task/CAS tables, intervention curves, computational-cost plot, and embedding-size ablations. Competitors were checked against primary arXiv or OpenReview records on 2026-08-23. The central contradiction audit distinguishes the supervised scalar score from the unsupervised degrees of freedom in each dynamic vector; findings labeled reviewer inference are not author claims.
